title: First and second conditional
tagline: Real plans for the future, or a world that is only in your imagination.
why: Every time you talk about a plan (If it rains, we'll stay in) or a dream (If I had a million dollars…), you need a conditional. B1 Preliminary tests the difference between the two in the reading cloze and expects you to use them naturally in your story and in the Speaking discussion. The number one B1 mistake is mixing the halves: If I would have… — and this topic fixes it for good.

hook.text: Saturday plans. Liam: "If it's sunny tomorrow, we'll go to the beach." Nadia: "And if I had a car, I'd drive us there in ten minutes!" Liam laughs: "You're fourteen. You can't drive." Nadia: "I said if…"
hook.ask: Liam's plan is real and possible. Nadia's idea is imaginary. Look at the verbs after if and after the comma: which tense does each one use, and why?

diagrams.title: The two halves of a conditional

sentences.note: first conditional: real — present simple + will
second conditional: imaginary — past simple + would
the if-half can go second — then no comma

diagrams.caption: The if-half never takes will or would. Those helpers live in the other half only.

rows.label: Result half
cells: will / won't + verb (or can, may, imperative)

rows.label: Example
cells: If I pass the exam, my parents will be happy.
If I were the head teacher, I would ban homework.

rows.label: How the speaker feels
cells: "This is just a dream — or advice."

diagrams.title: How to choose the right conditional

steps.label: Ask: is it possible?
steps.ex: Rain tomorrow? Possible → first. Me with a car at fourteen? No → second.

steps.label: Write the if-half with NO will/would
steps.ex: If it rains… / If I had a car…

steps.label: Add will (real) or would (imaginary) to the result
Comma only when if comes first
steps.ex: If it rains, we'll stay in. → We'll stay in if it rains.

head: Type
If-half
Result half
Use it for
rows: advice and instructions: If you're cold, put on a coat.

examples.text: If it rains on Saturday, the match will be cancelled.
You'll miss the bus if you don't hurry.
examples.note: a warning — if-half second, no comma

examples.text: If Sofia finishes early, she'll help us with the poster.
examples.note: a plan that depends on something

examples.text: I'll call you if I have any news.

use.point: First conditional with other results: can, may, imperatives

examples.text: If you're tired, go to bed early.
If we leave now, we can catch the seven o'clock train.
If the shop is open, buy some bread, please.

use.point: Second conditional: imaginary or unlikely situations

examples.text: If I had more free time, I'd learn the guitar.
If Mateo lived in Cusco, he'd visit Machu Picchu every weekend.
What would you do if you found a wallet in the street?
If dogs could talk, they'd complain about the cat.

use.point: Second conditional for advice: if I were you

examples.text: If I were you, I'd tell Miss Vega the truth.
examples.note: were with I — the polite, correct form

examples.text: If I were Liam, I wouldn't worry about the test.

watch_out.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay at home.
watch_out.right: If it rains, we will stay at home.
watch_out.why: No will in the if-half. The present simple already talks about the future here.

watch_out.wrong: If I would have a car, I would drive.
watch_out.right: If I had a car, I would drive.
watch_out.why: No would in the if-half either — past simple only.

watch_out.wrong: If I had a million dollars, I will buy a house.
watch_out.right: If I had a million dollars, I would buy a house.
watch_out.why: Past simple in the if-half needs would in the result — don't mix the two types.

watch_out.wrong: If I pass the exam I'll be happy, if I fail I'll try again.
watch_out.right: If I pass the exam, I'll be happy. If I fail, I'll try again.
watch_out.why: Comma after the if-half when it comes first, and a full stop between two sentences.

watch_out.wrong: If I was you, I'd study more.
watch_out.right: If I were you, I'd study more.
watch_out.why: If I were you is a fixed phrase; examiners expect were.

watch_out.wrong: If you'll help me, I'll help you.
watch_out.right: If you help me, I'll help you.
watch_out.why: Same rule again: after if, present simple — never will.

l1.es: Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa.
l1.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay at home.
l1.right: If it rains, we'll stay at home.
l1.why: Spanish uses the present after si too — copy that, and never add will.

l1.es: Si tuviera un coche, te llevaría.
l1.wrong: If I would have a car, I would take you.
l1.right: If I had a car, I'd take you.
l1.why: The Spanish -ra form becomes a plain past simple in English.

l1.wrong: What you would do if you win the lottery?
l1.right: What would you do if you won the lottery?
l1.why: Question order (would you do) and past simple after if.

remember.trick: No will, no would, after IF you should!
remember.tip: Cover the if-half with your finger: if you see will or would there, it's wrong. Real → present + will. Imaginary → past + would.

dialogue.title: The school trip vote
dialogue.context: The class has to choose between the beach and the mountains for the end-of-year trip. Nadia, Liam and Mateo argue about it at break time.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: If we choose the beach, we'll spend the whole day swimming.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: And if it's cloudy, we'll spend the whole day in the bus. The mountains are safer.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Honestly, if I had the choice, I'd stay at home and sleep.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: You would say that! If you came to the beach, you'd love it.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: OK, here's a deal. If the weather forecast is good, I'll vote for the beach.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Then we'll go to the mountains and you two can complain all day.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: If I were the teacher, I'd let us do both.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: If you were the teacher, Nadia, nobody would pass English.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Very funny. Come on — if we don't hurry, we'll miss the vote.

can_do: I can talk about a real plan or warning with if + present and will.
I can describe an imaginary situation with if + past and would.
I can give advice with If I were you, I'd… and choose the right conditional in a cloze.
summary: First conditional = real and possible: if + present simple, will + verb.
Second conditional = imaginary, unlikely or advice: if + past simple, would + verb.
Never put will or would after if — the helper lives in the result half.
The result half can also use can, may, an imperative (first) or could, might (second).
Comma when the if-half comes first; if I were you is the fixed advice phrase.
